planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring into gritty, well-drained, neutral to acidic soil tucked among rocks or at the base of a shaded ledge; this species rots quickly in heavy, poorly drained garden soil.

directions: Roundleaf catchfly is an Appalachian endemic that scrambles over shaded sandstone cliffs and rocky wooded slopes, sending up sticky, semi-trailing stems with rounded leaves and clusters of bright pink, deeply notched flowers from midsummer into fall. The sticky-glandular stems intercept crawling insects, hence the common name catchfly, while the open flowers are readily worked by bumblebees and other native bees drawn into the shaded understory. Because it is adapted to thin, rocky soil pockets and dislikes standing moisture, it performs best tucked into a rock garden crevice, dry shaded slope, or the gritty edge of a woodland path rather than a conventional border. It is an unusual, little-cultivated choice for gardeners wanting pollinator interest in dry shade where few other native forbs will thrive.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated transplants in spring into circumneutral, humus-rich forest soil in dappled to half-day shade beneath deciduous canopy; avoid wild collection since this species is globally rare.

directions: Blue Ridge catchfly is a rare, tall woodland perennial of rich cove forests over calcareous or mafic rock in the southern Appalachians, sending up slender, unbranched stalks topped with nodding, pale greenish-white flowers in late summer. The flowers stay closed through the day and open toward evening, releasing fragrance that draws in nectaring sphinx moths and other night-flying pollinators after dark. It is best grown in a shaded woodland garden with rich, well-drained loam and left undisturbed once established, since it resents root disturbance and takes a couple of seasons to reach flowering size. Growing this uncommon species in cultivation helps take pressure off its scattered, vulnerable wild populations.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall so it can cold-moist stratify over winter; the seed of this Apiaceae relative of golden alexanders germinates unevenly without a cold period.

directions: Hairy-jointed meadow parsnip is a close relative of golden alexanders, easily told apart by the tuft of fine hairs at its leaf joints, producing flat-topped clusters of small, pale yellow flowers in late spring that draw in a wide range of small native bees, flies, and beetles. It grows naturally along streambanks and in moist, partially shaded forest openings, making it a good companion for the sunnier-adapted Zizia aurea where a garden transitions from open ground into woodland edge. Like its Zizia relatives, it serves as a larval host for black swallowtail butterflies, extending host-plant availability into shadier parts of the garden. It tolerates a range of moisture levels once established but blooms most heavily with at least a few hours of direct or dappled sun.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring into well-drained, humus-rich woodland soil under deciduous shade.

directions: Curtis's goldenrod is a Southern and Central Appalachian endemic found deep in mountain forests, where it holds upright, gently arching stems of sharply toothed leaves topped by narrow, elongated plumes of bright yellow flowers from late summer into October. Unlike the more familiar sun-loving goldenrods, it thrives in part shade to fairly deep shade under a hardwood canopy, making it valuable for extending goldenrod-driven late-season nectar and pollen into shaded gardens where bees and migrating butterflies otherwise find slim pickings. It combines well with other shade goldenrods such as S. caesia and S. flexicaulis but has a more erect, less arching habit and coarser-toothed foliage, giving textural variety to a woodland native planting. Give it consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil and leave it undisturbed to slowly form long-lived clumps.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into moist, circumneutral bottomland or streamside soil in bright shade to filtered sun.

directions: Eared goldenrod is a clump-forming, non-spreading woodland goldenrod of the south-central and southeastern US, named for the small ear-like lobes clasping the leaf bases, producing sprays of small bright-yellow flowers in late summer and fall. It grows naturally along streamsides and in rocky or alluvial bottomland forests, and unlike many goldenrods it holds up well in fairly deep shade without becoming leggy, making it a dependable choice for a shaded rain garden or stream-edge planting. Its late bloom period provides an important nectar and pollen source for bees and migrating butterflies at a time when shaded areas of the garden typically offer little else in flower. Because it forms tidy clumps rather than running by rhizome like S. caesia or S. flexicaulis, it is easier to place in a mixed woodland border without it wandering into neighboring plants.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for winter stratification into lean, well-drained soil under open deciduous or oak canopy; this aster tolerates dry shade better than most and does not want rich, damp beds.

directions: Wavyleaf aster is easily recognized by its heart-shaped, wavy-margined leaves that clasp the stem, and by its unusual tolerance for dry, upland woodland conditions where most native asters struggle without supplemental moisture. From August through November it produces abundant small lavender flowers with yellow centers along branching, sprawling stems, providing a critical late-season nectar source for bees and migrating butterflies in dry shaded and part-shaded woodland edges. It thrives in the lean, well-drained soil of open oak-hickory forest and roadbanks, making it a practical choice for a naturalized dry shade garden where wetter-adapted asters would fail. Cut it back by half in early summer if a bushier, more compact form is desired for garden use.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich loam at a woodland edge with dappled to partial shade.

directions: Crooked-stem aster takes its name from its zigzagging stems clasped by narrow, tapering leaves, producing a profusion of pale lavender, yellow-centered flowers in late summer and fall that draw large numbers of native bees and butterflies into the variable light of a woodland edge or streambank. It grows naturally in the dappled shade of thickets, wood margins, and moist banks, thriving where sun exposure shifts through the day rather than in constant deep shade or full sun. Beyond its nectar value, it serves as a larval host for the Pearl Crescent and Silvery Checkerspot butterflies, giving it ecological value beyond flowering. Plant it along a part-shade border or rain garden margin where its arching, gently zigzagging stems can be appreciated up close.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
